# How to Send a Quick Voice Message to a Family Member's Echo

> **In short:** With Alexa+, you can speak a short voice note to one Echo and have it play out loud on another Echo in your home, hands-free. Amazon says Alexa+ understands more conversational wording than the older Alexa, so you can name a room or a person in plain English. Note: Alexa+ is still rolling out — if your Echo doesn't have it yet, the older "Drop In" command still works with similar steps.

You're downstairs chopping vegetables. Your partner is upstairs with headphones on, and the kids have a movie blaring. Yelling doesn't work, and walking up costs you time and a clean knife hand. A short voice note dropped on the bedroom Echo solves it in about ten seconds. This guide walks you through that — naming the right Echo, speaking your message, and checking it actually arrived.

One honest limit up front: this is a one-shot voice note, not a phone call. The other person can't talk back through the Echo, and if their device is on Do Not Disturb, the message will arrive silently in the Alexa app instead of playing out loud.

## Before you start
- **Two Echo devices**, both signed in and on the same Amazon household (or a family member's account that has accepted you as a contact). One is the speaker, one is the receiver.
- **The Alexa app** (free on iOS or Android), already installed and signed in on your phone.
- **Clear names for each Echo** in the app — something like "Kitchen Echo" and "Bedroom Echo" — so Alexa can tell them apart.
- **Communications turned on** in the app. It usually is by default, but if it was ever disabled, you'll need to switch it back.
- **About 5 minutes** the first time, around 30 seconds once you've done it a few times.
- **A quick honesty note:** if you only have one Echo, this guide doesn't apply yet — you need a second device to receive the message. Also, Alexa+ features are still reaching devices in waves; if a step doesn't match your screen, the older "Drop In" command may be what your Echo understands instead.

## Step 1 — Name each Echo so Alexa can tell them apart
Open the **Alexa app** on your phone. At the bottom of the screen, look for a tab that has a small speaker or chip icon — this is usually labeled **Devices**. When you tap it, you'll see a list of every Echo on your account. If two of them have the same generic name, tap the one you want to rename, then look for an **Edit** option (often labeled "Edit Name" or shown as a small pencil icon) and give it a room-based name.
💬 Example name pair: "Kitchen Echo" and "Bedroom Echo."
**If it looks different:** the Devices tab sometimes lives under a **Menu** button (three lines, often in the top-left corner). If you can't find a rename option, your device may not be on the Alexa+ rollout yet — the older "Drop In" command works the same way and uses the same names.
You'll know it worked when both Echos appear in the app with clearly different, location-based names.

## Step 2 — Make sure the recipient is in your Alexa contacts
Still in the Alexa app, look at the bottom bar for a tab that has a chat-bubble or speech-bubble icon — this is often labeled **Communicate**, though some accounts see **Talk** or **Message** instead. Tap it, then look near the top for **Contacts**. You should see the family member you want to message if you've ever called or messaged them through Alexa before. If they're not there, look for an **Add Contact** button and follow the prompts to add them by name or by their Amazon account email.
💬 Example: add "Mom" with her Amazon account email so her Echo shows up under that name.
**If it looks different:** if you only see your own devices and no contacts, communications may be turned off. Look in the app under **Settings → Alexa Account → Alexa Communications** (or something similar) and switch it on.
You'll know it worked when you can see the family member's name in your contacts list, with at least one of their Echo devices listed underneath.

## Step 3 — Send a voice note by speaking to your Echo
Walk over to the Echo you want to send **from** and say the wake word — usually "Alexa" — followed by your request in plain language. Amazon says Alexa+ is designed to understand more conversational phrasing than the older Alexa, so you don't need to memorize a rigid command. Just describe what you want the way you'd describe it to a person.
💬 Example phrases: "Alexa, drop a voice message on the Kitchen Echo." / "Alexa, send a voice message to Mom's Echo saying dinner is ready." / "Alexa, tell the Bedroom Echo we'll leave in five minutes."
**If it looks different:** if you only have one Echo in your home, Alexa may say she can't find the device you named — go back to Step 1 and make sure the names match what you actually said. If the older "Drop In" wording is what your Echo understands, that still works; the rest of the steps below behave the same way.
You'll know it worked when Alexa confirms out loud — something like "Sending your message to the Kitchen Echo" — and you hear a short chime.

## Step 4 — Speak your note, then stop talking to send it
After the chime, just talk naturally — a short sentence is plenty. Think of it like leaving a voice memo on someone's answering machine: keep it short, speak clearly, and stop. There's no "send" button. Stopping talking is what sends it. If you pause for a moment after your message, Alexa wraps up the recording and ships it.
💬 Example: "Hey, dinner's on the table — come down when you can."
**If it looks different:** if the recording seems to keep going longer than you'd like, just stay quiet for a beat and it will close on its own. If your message gets cut off mid-sentence because you paused too long, just say the command again and try once more — speaking in one smooth go usually works best.
You'll know it worked when Alexa says something like "Message sent" and the Echo's light ring returns to its normal idle color (usually blue, then off).

## Step 5 — Check on the receiving Echo
On the Echo that's supposed to play your message, the voice note will play out loud automatically when it arrives. The light ring usually pulses while it's playing, so anyone nearby knows a message just dropped. If you're curious whether it landed, open the **Alexa app**, go back to the **Communicate** tab, and look for a **Recent** or **Conversations** list — your voice drop should appear with the recipient Echo's name and the time it was sent.
💬 Example: send "Test from the kitchen" the first time you set this up, then walk to the other Echo and confirm you heard it play.
**If it looks different:** if the recipient Echo is muted or has **Do Not Disturb** turned on, the message still arrives in the Alexa app but won't play out loud on the device. Open the app, tap that Echo, and look for a **Do Not Disturb** toggle to switch it off if needed.
You'll know it worked when the receiving Echo plays your words out loud in Alexa's voice, or when the entry shows up in your Recent list with the right device name and time.

## Common mistakes
- **Both Echos have the same name.** If everything is just "Echo," Alexa can't tell them apart and will either ask a clarifying question or send to the wrong one. Rename each device with its room (Step 1).
- **The recipient isn't in your contacts.** You can only send a voice message to someone who has accepted your contact request in the Alexa app. Add them through the Communicate tab first, then have them accept on their end.
- **Do Not Disturb is on the receiving Echo.** The message still arrives but stays silent. Turn off Do Not Disturb in the Alexa app, or say "Alexa, turn off Do Not Disturb" on that specific Echo.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** a quick voice drop replaces the "yell upstairs" routine, the "send a text" friction, and the "find my phone" scramble. It's also handy for relatives who prefer talking to typing — kids, older parents, anyone who'd rather hear your voice than read a message.
- **For your business or work:** if you run a small home business, you can drop a voice note from your office Echo to a workshop or garage Echo without leaving what you're doing — useful when your hands are full or you're mid-task.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is renaming your two most-used Echos with their room names. Once that's done, every future voice drop is a single sentence away.

## Try it now
Pick two Echos in your home, give them clear room names in the Alexa app, and send one short test message between them. Time yourself — most people land their first successful drop in under a minute once the names are set.
